opus-5.5.text:
I think the honest answer is: carefully, and with a lot of humility in both directions.

There's a tempting move people make where they say, well, these models are trained on next-token prediction, which is obviously not what children do, so they can't tell us anything about people. And there's an equally tempting move in the other direction, where because a model produces fluent language, people assume it must be doing something human-like inside. I don't think either of those is right.

The way I tend to think about it is that language models are a kind of existence proof. For a long time in cognitive science and linguistics, there were arguments of the form "you could never learn X from text alone," or "you need some specific built-in structure to acquire Y." And now we have systems that, whatever else is true about them, acquire a surprising amount of grammatical knowledge, some world knowledge, some ability to do certain kinds of reasoning, just from exposure to a lot of text. That doesn't mean humans learn the same way. Kids get vastly less linguistic input, they're grounded in a physical and social world, they have goals and communicative intent. But it does change what counts as a plausible argument about what's learnable in principle, and that's a genuinely useful thing for the science.

The second thing is that these models are something we can actually open up and poke at. With people, we have behavioral experiments and some neuroimaging, but we can't intervene on individual representations very precisely. With a model, we can ask: is there something in here that looks like a representation of the state of the world being described? Does it track who knows what in a story? And we can intervene and see if the behavior changes. A lot of my group's work has been on questions like that, whether models build something like a situation model or a model of the speaker's beliefs and goals. When we find structure like that, it's a hypothesis generator. It suggests representational solutions that might also be worth looking for in brains, or at least it tells us those solutions are reachable by a learning process.

Where I get more cautious is the step from "the model and the human produce similar outputs" to "they're doing the same computation." That's where you really need targeted experiments, places where different underlying mechanisms predict different patterns of errors or different generalization. Humans make very particular mistakes, and the interesting comparisons are often in the failures rather than the successes.

So I'd say the models are most useful to me not as models of humans, exactly, but as a new kind of object that sharpens our questions. They force you to be precise about what you think is special about human language and thought, because you now have to explain why this thing that does a lot of it is still different.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the first thing to say is that I'm pretty cautious about reading these models as direct models of human cognition. They're trained on a very different kind of data, with a very different objective, and in a very different quantity than anything a child is exposed to. So if you ask "is GPT-whatever a model of the human language faculty," my honest answer is mostly no, or at least not in the way a cognitive scientist would want.

But I think that framing misses what's actually interesting. The more useful way to think about it is as an existence proof. For a long time there were debates in linguistics and cognitive science that went something like, "you couldn't possibly acquire this structure from distributional evidence alone, therefore it must be innate." And what these models show is that a lot of that structure, things like hierarchical syntax, agreement over long distances, some aspects of semantics, is in fact recoverable from text alone, given enough of it. That doesn't tell you that humans do it that way. But it does take certain poverty-of-the-stimulus arguments off the table, or at least forces people to make them much more carefully and quantitatively.

The second thing I'd say is that they're useful as tools for asking questions about representation. If you have a system that's clearly doing something language-like, you can go inside it and ask, is there anything that looks like a part-of-speech tag, is there anything that looks like a syntactic tree, is there anything that looks like a world model? And then you can ask whether the same kinds of representational commitments show up in human data, in behavioral experiments or neural data. There's been some nice work correlating model representations with brain recordings during language comprehension. I'm a little skeptical of how far that goes, but it's at least a hypothesis-generating machine.

And then the third thing, which I actually find most interesting, is where they fail. The places where models are very fluent but clearly don't have a coherent picture of what they're talking about, that's where you learn something about what humans have in addition to statistical regularities over text. Things like grounding, things like having a persistent model of a situation, things like actually caring about whether what you said is true. Those gaps are informative. They tell you which pieces of intelligence aren't just a byproduct of predicting the next word.

So the summary is, I don't treat them as models of people, I treat them as a comparison class. They're the first systems that are fluent enough that the comparison is actually meaningful, and the differences are where the science is.

astra-6.text:
I think they’re useful in part because they challenge our intuitions about what kinds of learning are possible. You might look at some aspect of human language use and say, well, acquiring that must require a particular innate structure, or direct experience of the world. If a model learns something resembling that behavior from text, that’s a reason to revisit the claim. It shows that there may be more information in the learning signal than we thought.

But there’s a big gap between showing that a behavior can emerge in a language model and explaining how it emerges in a person. The models get very different training data, in very different quantities, and they learn under very different conditions. So success on the same task doesn’t establish that they’re using the same mechanism.

What I find most promising is treating these models as a way to make hypotheses concrete. We can vary the data or the learning setup, see what abilities emerge, and compare both the successes and the errors with human behavior. That can help us ask sharper questions about human intelligence, even when the model itself turns out to be a poor account of how people learn.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we have to be careful about what kind of inference we’re making. The fact that a language model can do something that looks like what a person does doesn’t necessarily mean it’s doing it in the same way. These systems are trained on very different amounts of data, with very different learning objectives, from the ones that humans encounter.

But they’re useful as existence proofs. If you can learn some behavior just by predicting text, that tells us something about the information available in language and the kinds of structure a learner can recover from it. It might challenge a claim that a particular ability requires some very specific innate machinery. It doesn’t establish that humans acquire that ability in the same way.

So I’m most excited about using these models to formulate more precise hypotheses: where do their generalizations line up with human generalizations, where do they diverge, and what changes to the data or the learning process explain that difference? That seems like a productive way to turn their successes—and their failures—into something we can test about human intelligence.
